title: Signed Voltage Sensitivity and Trip-Aware Positive-Neighbour Control for Photovoltaic Hosting Capacity in a Four-Wire Rural Low-Voltage Network
content: Photovoltaic hosting capacity in low-voltage (LV) networks is usually assessed with balanced or three-wire models, although much of European rural distribution is four-wire with predominantly single-phase connections, where the neutral couples the phases and the voltage response to an injection depends on the phase of the injecting unit. This paper derives that dependence in closed form and builds a coordinated curtailment scheme on it. The test system is a 250 kVA rural substation in north-eastern Romania with 213 supply points, 95.3% of them single-phase, and 53 prosumers, whose feeder, pole and phase are taken from operator records. A four-wire power flow including the EN 50549-1 trip and reconnection sequence compares six inverter strategies with a proposed Trip-Aware Positive-Neighbour Control (PNC), in which the operator releases a per-inverter power ceiling at each averaging window and tightens it only on units with positive voltage sensitivity. The critical-node sensitivity is +3.294 V/kW on the injecting phase and negative on the other two, so only 35 of the 53 units can relieve it, and its sign depends on the power factor. Reactive absorption drives the non-generating phases to 202.0 V at midday. PNC and a local P(U) droop both reach 500 kWp, twice the transformer rating, but PNC curtails 23% less energy and keeps a Jain fairness index of 0.930 against 0.850. Prosumer phase allocation alone is worth 44% of the curtailed energy.
